Sources: istanbul/AUTHORITY-MAP-ISTANBUL.md + SPEED-RULES-ISTANBUL.md + DEMAND-POOLS-ISTANBUL.md + FARE-BENCHMARKS-ISTANBUL.md + NODES-ISTANBUL.md + REVENUE-INPUTS-ISTANBUL.md. CONTRACT v3: only `title` (<=6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (<=140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Underscore-prefixed fields NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Posture per the framing rule in AUTHORITY-MAP-ISTANBUL.md: Istanbul runs one of the world's great ferry systems — Navier NEVER frames itself as introducing water transit; the page leads with the city's own operations and published climate plan, and the ask is a fast, low-wake, zero-emission EXPRESS tier that grows the water's share of cross-strait trips. Operate-first dual posture (İBB both operates and licenses). Speed honesty is the defining constraint and renders plainly: 10 kn over-ground inside the strait, network anchored south of it; the cross-strait shuttle is a comfort tier with no time claim; Golden Horn excluded. No counterparty identities, no program or fleet commitments, no partnership claims (Şehir Hatları/İDO/Dentur/Turyol are landscape facts only), no launch dates, no service-start years.

fn1.text: Şehir Hatları, the city's own ferry operator, in its own words: 53 piers, 30 vessels, about 903 sailings a day, and around 40 million passengers a year.

fn2.text: The İstanbul Climate Change Action Plan, as published by the metropolitan municipality: carbon-neutral by 2050, with interim absolute-reduction targets of −52% by 2030 and −89% by 2040.

fn3.text: Cross-strait shares from municipal figures as reported for 2025: the rail tunnel line averaged about 607,000 riders a day and the bus rapid transit line about 748,000, while the city ferries carry about 40 million riders a year — roughly 110,000 a day. Water today carries a low-single-digit share of cross-strait trips.

fn4.text: Speed limits in these waters are set by the Turkish Straits traffic regulation (Presidential Decree No. 1426) and the Istanbul Harbor Master's local marine traffic guide: 10 knots over the ground for all vessels inside the strait, with fast craft expressly held to that limit north of the harbor line, and a 4-knot rule in defined zones. South of the harbor line, on the open Marmara, no blanket cap applies. All times on this page respect every limit on a conservative planning basis — no speed allowance is assumed anywhere.

fn5.text: In December 2024 the Istanbul Harbor Master documented, in an official letter, serious wake damage to moored vessels caused by fast craft in the Golden Horn, directing that masters be continuously warned. Local traffic rules also cap vessel noise at 85 decibels. A foilborne electric vessel produces minimal wake at speed and runs near-silent — the letter's concern, answered by design. The Golden Horn is not part of this network.

fn6.text: The city's published fare ladder, per the February 2026 tariff update as reported: a 42-lira base transit fare, cross-strait ferry fares of about 53–65 lira ($1.1–1.4), Islands fares up to about 206 lira ($4.3), and the city's own on-demand sea taxi priced above them under a published tariff. Lira fares are revised several times a year; lira figures convert at 47.76 lira per dollar, the central bank's indicative rate at preparation, and are indicative only.

fn7.text: Tourism figures for 2025: Türkiye received 63.9 million visitors and $65.2 billion in tourism revenue per the national statistics office; İstanbul led the country with about 17.5 million foreign visitors, and the city's ports handled more than 625,000 cruise passengers, per ministry year-end data as reported.

fn8.text: İstanbul's registered population is 15,655,924 (national address-based registry, 2024).

fn9.text: Navier times are computed from route distance at each segment's legal speed, with conservative approach and dwell allowances at every call. Road and existing-schedule comparisons are traffic- and season-dependent indications, not measurements.

gap.title: Istanbul has already published the plan

copy.lead: This city is not waiting to be convinced about water transport — it runs one of the world's great ferry systems: 53 piers, about 903 sailings a day, around 40 million riders a year, and its own on-demand sea taxi above the ferry fares. What the water is missing is speed on the axes the road serves worst.
copy.support: Water today carries a low-single-digit share of cross-strait trips — the rail tunnel alone moves about 607,000 riders a day. A fast, low-wake, zero-emission express tier grows the water's share on trips the ferries serve slowly or not at all — the Marmara shore axis and the car-free Islands — in service of the city's own carbon-neutral 2050 plan.

copy.framing: One conversation, not two. Istanbul already operates one of the world's most-used urban water networks and licenses private operators beside it — the posture here is extension: a fast, zero-emission express tier above the ferry system the city already runs, and toward the climate targets the city has already published.
copy.enable_track: License the tier: line permission, tariff terms and pier access sit with the city's own transport authority. Private capital finances the vessels — the ask is licensing and landings, not money.
copy.operate_track: Bring the vessels inside the city's family — a premium express product above the ferry network, run the way the city already runs its sea taxi, counted toward its own climate and ridership goals.

operate_proof_points.proof: Plans and coordinates all city transport, owns the ferry operator and the on-demand sea taxi, and decides routes, tariffs and line permissions for scheduled water transport through its own transport authority.
53 piers, 30 vessels, about 903 sailings a day and around 40 million riders a year — one of the world's great ferry operations, and the pier inventory these waters already have.
Carbon-neutral by 2050 with −52% by 2030 — a zero-emission express tier is additive capacity toward targets the city has already set.

Never framed as replacing the ferries; the ferry triangle the city serves superbly is deliberately not overlaid. Private-operator precedent (İDO/Dentur/Turyol) supports the Enable track as landscape fact — no partnership claims.

pillars: Zero-emission electric foiling — measurable progress toward the city's carbon-neutral 2050 plan, on the water where the city already leads.
Minimal wake and near-silent at speed — the stated purposes of the strait's speed and noise rules, served by design.
Time returned on the axes the road serves worst — the Marmara shore and the car-free Islands — and a visitor economy joined to the water.

copy.headline: The strait's rules are the design brief.
copy.framing: Inside the Bosphorus, every vessel is held to 10 knots over the ground — so this network puts its speed where the rules allow it: the open Marmara and the Islands. The purposes behind the strait's rules — wake, noise, safety — are what a foiling electric vessel is built to serve.
copy.ask: No speed allowance is assumed anywhere on this page. Cross-strait legs run at the limit, hull-borne, sold as comfort and zero emissions — never as a time claim. Where the city wishes to measure wake and noise, we welcome the measurement.

expander.title: Why the network lives south of the strait
body: The strait regulations cap all traffic at 10 knots over the ground inside the Bosphorus, and fast craft are expressly held to that limit north of the harbor line. South of it, on the open Marmara, no blanket cap applies — so the trunk line and the Islands express run at full service speed, where the hydrofoil's advantage is decisive, and the cross-strait shuttle stays an honest comfort tier at the same speed as today's ferries.

The Harbor Master's own December 2024 letter documents serious wake damage to moored vessels from fast craft in the Golden Horn. A foilborne electric vessel produces minimal wake at speed and runs near-silent — the concern in that letter, answered by design. The Golden Horn itself is not part of this network: its harbor rules and the protection of moored vessels make it unsuitable for fast service, and we honor that.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 30 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: Istanbul's water-transport landscape is deep and clearly governed. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Plans and coordinates public transport city-wide; owns the ferry operator and the on-demand sea taxi; routes, tariffs and line permissions for scheduled city water transport are decided through its own transport authority. Steward of the carbon-neutral 2050 plan.
The city's ferry operator: 53 piers, 30 vessels, about 903 sailings a day and around 40 million riders a year across the strait, the Islands and the tour lines — the pier inventory of these waters.

The national maritime layer: vessel registration and flag, survey and certification, and crew licensing. Its Istanbul Harbor Master administers the port area, publishes the local marine traffic guide, and holds the strait's speed and noise rules.
Operates the strait's vessel traffic services and pilotage and announces current and closure conditions — the operational safety layer every schedule on this page respects.
